terms.comment: We have found no ancient interjection for a bark; bau is the sound in Lucretius’s baubārī (below).
Of dogs left alone in an empty house; Lewis & Short sets it against lātrāre, to bark angrily.

evidence: Lewis & Short: not before the Augustan age
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: not before the Augustan period, and then mostly of people, “to assail with harsh words”.

evidence: Verg. G. 3.411: latrātū turbābis agēns (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: heus, inquit, linguam vīs meam praeclūdere, nē lātrem prō rē dominī?
phrases.english: “Hey,” he said, “do you want to stop my mouth, so that I won’t bark to guard my master’s goods?”

sources: Lewis & Short: latro · Lewis & Short: baubor
Phaedrus from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-phaedrus).
The example sentence marked “composed” is ours.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 277.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
